content: A lens is an optical device that transmits and refracts light, either converging or diverging the light beam. It typically exhibits axial symmetry, meaning its structure is symmetrical around a central axis. A simple lens consists of a single optical element, while a compound lens is made up of multiple simple lenses aligned along a common axis. The use of multiple elements in a compound lens allows for the correction of more optical aberrations than a single lens element can achieve. Lenses are commonly manufactured from materials such as glass or transparent plastic. Lenses can also refract electromagnetic radiation outside the visible spectrum. For example, a microwave lens can be made from paraffin wax. The term lens originates from the Latin word for lentil, as the shape of a double-convex lens resembles that of a lentil seed. Historically, lenses have been used for various purposes, with early examples including a rock crystal lens found in Nineveh (circa 640 BC) and references to burning glasses in Ancient Greece, such as in Aristophanes' play The Clouds (424 BC). These burning glasses were biconvex lenses used to focus sunlight to ignite fires. The Roman Empire also recognized the utility of lenses, as described by Pliny the Elder. Nero, for instance, reportedly used an emerald, likely concave, to correct myopia while watching gladiatorial games. Both Pliny and Seneca the Younger noted the magnifying effects of a glass globe filled with water. The scientific understanding of lenses advanced significantly with the work of Ibn al-Haytham (965–1038), who wrote the Book of Optics, describing how the lens in the human eye forms an image on the retina. In the 11th and 12th centuries, the Vikings produced high-quality rock crystal lenses, known as Visby lenses, which were capable of focusing sunlight to ignite fires and had imaging qualities comparable to modern aspheric lenses from the 1950s. The widespread use of lenses began with the introduction of reading stones in the 11th century and the invention of spectacles in Italy during the 1280s. Nicholas of Cusa is credited with discovering the benefits of concave lenses for correcting myopia in 1451. The design of optical instruments was revolutionized in the 1860s by Ernst Abbe, who formulated the Abbe sine condition. This principle ensures that lenses produce sharp images of both on-axis and off-axis objects, leading to significant advancements in devices like microscopes. Abbe's work also contributed to the establishment of the Carl Zeiss company as a leading manufacturer of optical instruments. Most lenses are spherical, meaning their surfaces are segments of spheres. These surfaces can be convex (bulging outward), concave (curving inward), or planar (flat). The line connecting the centers of the spheres that form the lens surfaces is called the lens axis. Lenses can be modified after manufacturing by cutting or grinding to achieve different shapes or sizes, which may alter the position of the lens axis. Toric or spherocylindrical lenses have surfaces with two different radii of curvature in orthogonal planes, resulting in varying focal powers in different meridians. This design introduces deliberate astigmatism. Aspheric lenses, on the other hand, have surfaces that are neither spherical nor cylindrical, allowing them to produce images with significantly reduced aberrations compared to standard lenses. Lenses are classified based on the curvature of their optical surfaces. A biconvex lens has two convex surfaces, while a biconcave lens has two concave surfaces. A plano-convex lens has one flat and one convex surface, and a plano-concave lens has one flat and one concave surface. A convex-concave lens, or meniscus lens, has one convex and one concave surface. Meniscus lenses are commonly used in corrective eyewear and can be either positive or negative, depending on the relative curvatures of their surfaces. The focal length of a lens is the distance from the lens to the point where a collimated beam of light converges (for positive lenses) or appears to diverge (for negative lenses). The optical power of a lens, measured in diopters, is the reciprocal of its focal length in meters. Positive lenses focus light to a real image, while negative lenses create virtual images that cannot be projected onto a screen but can be observed through the lens. Aberrations, or imperfections in image formation, are inherent to all lenses. Spherical aberration occurs because spherical surfaces are not the ideal shape for focusing light, leading to blurring. This can be minimized by using aspheric lenses or carefully selecting the curvature of the lens surfaces. Coma, another type of aberration, affects off-axis objects and results in comet-like flares in the image. Chromatic aberration arises from the dispersion of the lens material, causing different wavelengths of light to focus at different points. This can be reduced using achromatic doublets or apochromatic lenses, which combine materials with different dispersive properties. Compound lenses, which consist of multiple simple lenses, are used to correct optical aberrations. These lenses can be arranged in contact or separated by a distance, with their combined focal length determined by their individual focal lengths and separation. Compound lenses are employed in various optical systems, including telescopes, microscopes, and cameras. Lenses have numerous applications, from magnifying glasses and corrective eyewear to imaging systems like binoculars, telescopes, and cameras. Convex lenses can concentrate sunlight to a focal point, generating enough heat to ignite materials. This principle is used in solar energy systems to focus light onto photovoltaic cells, increasing energy efficiency. Lenses are also utilized in radio astronomy and radar systems to refract electromagnetic radiation into collector antennas, as seen in the Square Kilometre Array radio telescope.
